title: Bernie and Lorna from Kumsheen Rafting
text:
They started their business 50 years (to the day) before we arrived!
Adele: Entrepreneurship is hard work - with or without employees. Remain focused on vision. Start small than expand. Listen to all stakeholders but must develop the ability to know whom to listen too.
Su: When no one has heard of river rafting and even question the sustainability of the business, they were firm believers of their own passion, overcoming obstacles and eventually build up the adventure tourism in Lytton and go on to create awareness on the importance of river ecology and the effect of climate change on Thomson River. And when the wild forest fire engulfed Lytton they immediately begin rebuilding, knowing many families depend on Kumsheen to put food on their tables.
Trish: Having a community helps people get through the difficult times - theater, art, music programs provide a place to gather, be together, be involved
Nicole: Community focused business can still be profitable and provide a great place to work. Kumsheen rafting is a family owned for-profit business which caters to the need of the community. Bank burned down = Scotiabank temporary bank on property. Forestry worker housing burnt down = open up space on property. Company pushing government to take action by staying involved and holding inaction accountable.

title: Jenna from Squamish
text: Kai: A critical component to success is community focused collaboration. There is always a balance that exists between having the right actors at the table who can understand impacts and with the authority to make decisions. I see an inverse relationship between quality decision making and distance to the impacted community. We saw a number of different communities responding to challenges and opportunities in BC.  An example that struck me was in Squamish, where Councillor Jenna Stoner told us how the progressive municipal government was working closely with the province, private organizations, traditional land owners and local residents to drive mutual value to progress the community. An example of this was a collaborative and engaging approach which resulted in mandating all residential developments contain a 15% affordable housing component, addressing a large prevalent issue. This approach could also be seen through the Lakeland Mills community and government engagement to drive more sustainable logging and milling practices. I have felt the frustration of not being consulted in my own work which has led to ineffective project delivery and economic and social implications. Reflecting on this, I have probably erred on the side of over consultation. This has a negative impact on  quality and expediency of decisions and actions. This is going to be something I continue to wrestle with to achieve the best outcome possible You can have a large scale impact by truly understanding the issue at the heart and starting local but it’s very hard to have a meaningful community impact when starting too big and without a deep understanding of the local context.

title: Dinner in Jasper
text:
Muhammed: During the dinner with Todd, Greg the Fire Chief,/a> and other Jasper community leaders, we gained valuable insights into forest wildfire management (from Landon Shepherd, a fire and vegetation specialist with Parks Canada) and the importance of community engagement. Todd's team's dedication and commitment to protecting the wilderness while actively involving the local community were truly inspiring. Their stories reminded us of the power of collaboration and the positive impact it can have on both nature and society after making Jasper home 25-30 years ago. Additionally, I was captivated by those who came to Jasper for holidays and ended up staying indefinitely. This exemplified the profound effect that a place like Jasper can have on people, drawing them in with its charm and creating a deep sense of belonging.
Kai: Not enough is being done in Jasper to drive diversity, opportunities, change. Pale male and stale

title: Heating in Prince George
text: We met the Mayor of Prince George, Simon Yu. who has had a fascinating journey from his birthplace in Hong Kong. He showed us the heating facility that uses the waste heat from the sawmill kiln, itself powered by waste sawdust, to heat 13 of the government buildings in their community. The tangible success of this pilot is being used to inspire and drive expansion. He also gave us some Prince George branded socks with the town's slightly terrifying mascot on them.

title: Bus Breakdown
text:
On the way to the glacier, the bus broke down because it was overheating. It was lovely how many people stopped and offered to help, including one guy in an interestingly decorated car with a doll strapped to the hood. We made it to a rest area and there we managed to get a lift with a lovely tour bus of Germans who took us to the Glacier and Skywalk.
Kali: Resilience and adaptability are sure signs of a great leader and are valuable in every facet of life. We had a testing journey that would have broken many teams apart, however we had fun, trusted the process and each other, and took all the challenges as they came. Regardless of the drama, I had the best day yesterday! Also, when you need to hitchhike and catch a random bus with strangers, call Ed :)
Caroline: The best decision for a team (or organization) isn’t always the perfect decision. Some sacrifices have to be made and some risks taken in order to reap some (or more) benefits. Like leaving our luggage behind! I know not everyone was comfortable with it and some even thought it was a bad idea. At that point our options were:  A) status quo or B) take a leap of faith. I imagine that the rest of the day would have turned out very different had we not taken that leap of faith to leave our luggage behind.
